name: Eszopiclone

lead: Eszopiclone (Lunesta) is a prescription sleeping pill for insomnia and the active half of zopiclone. In recovery circles, better sleep is tied to less puffiness, clearer skin and a fresher-looking face.
It enhances GABA-A receptor signalling near the benzodiazepine site, producing sedation. Approved by the FDA in 2004, it has been studied for insomnia; appearance outcomes have not been studied.

paras: It is taken at bedtime on prescription for insomnia, typically alongside sleep-hygiene measures. People using it for recovery describe the goal as falling and staying asleep more reliably so rest builds up over nights.

The FDA boxed warning (added 2019) covers complex sleep behaviors such as sleepwalking and sleep-driving. Other reported effects include next-day impairment, dependence and mood changes. It is Schedule IV in the US and prescription-only.

angle.text: Eszopiclone (Lunesta) is a prescription Z-drug for insomnia. The chain people describe is deeper, longer sleep, better overnight recovery, then clearer skin, less puffiness and a more rested face. Its research is in insomnia.

lead: Eszopiclone, sold as Lunesta and as generics, is a prescription nonbenzodiazepine hypnotic of the cyclopyrrolone class. It is the active (S)-enantiomer of zopiclone and is used for insomnia in adults.[1]

The FDA approved it in December 2004. It is a Schedule IV controlled substance in the US, and the FDA added a boxed warning in 2019 about serious injuries from complex sleep behaviors such as sleepwalking.[1]
Eszopiclone has no approved appearance use and no published studies of appearance outcomes. It is mentioned here as part of the sleep-medicine landscape that some people connect with recovery.

paras: Eszopiclone is indicated for the treatment of insomnia in adults.[1][2] The American Academy of Sleep Medicine guideline for chronic insomnia assessed individual drugs including eszopiclone.[3]

Its hypnotic effect is believed to arise from interaction with GABA-A receptor complexes near or coupled to benzodiazepine binding sites, enhancing inhibitory neurotransmission; the precise mechanism is described as unknown.[1][2] It is rapidly absorbed and has a half-life of about six hours.[1]

Labelled risks include CNS depression with next-day impairment, complex sleep behaviors (sleep-driving, sleepwalking), abnormal thinking or hallucinations, and worsening depression or suicidal ideation.[1][2] The FDA lowered the recommended starting dose in 2013 and added a boxed warning in 2019.[1] As a Schedule IV drug it carries risks of abuse, dependence and withdrawal.[1]

A randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled study tested nightly eszopiclone for six months in adults with chronic insomnia.[4] Other studies examined co-administration with fluoxetine in insomnia with major depression, and effects on respiratory arousal threshold in obstructive sleep apnoea.[5][6] A registered trial compared eszopiclone with zopiclone.[7]

A network meta-analysis in The Lancet compared pharmacological treatments for acute and long-term insomnia.[8] A matched cohort study associated hypnotic use with higher mortality, and reviews discuss safety in older adults; observational findings cannot establish cause.[9][10] No studies of appearance outcomes were found.
